Issued at 205 AM MDT Thu Oct 29 2026

Early this morning, I am listening to old school rhythm and
blues. When I turned to the station, it was a rather convenient
coincidence that the first song I listened to describes the 
weather across much of the area today. Shortwave ridging will 
build across the area today, and bring a dry day with above 
normal temperatures for late October. Some mid to high level 
clouds will move in at times, but nothing other than that. If 
you are still wondering about what the song that describes the 
weather today, it is "Lovely Day" by the late, great Bill 
Withers. So if you can, get out an enjoy it. Dry weather will 
continue through tonight, but more clouds may keep temperatures 
a bit warmer than Wednesday night.

The pattern begins getting more active following today. Clouds will 
increase Friday as moisture deepens ahead of a shortwave moving in 
from the southwest. Guidance continues to trend slower with the wave 
though. Most of the area will have a dry Friday with another day of 
above normal temperatures. Some locations, like Casper, will be well 
up into the 60s. As for precipitation, we can't rule out a shower in 
southwestern Wyoming. However, the chance is less than 1 out of 6 
and most showers would not occur until after sunset Friday night.

Guidance has also trended somewhat drier for Saturday. The main 
showers will be across western and southern Wyoming again, with 
diminishing chances further north and east. But even in the west, 
amounts look rather light, generally a tenth of an inch or less. 
Although the forecast East of the Divide is dry right now, we
can't rule out a shower in some locations. Chances are rather 
low at this time though, generally less than 1 out of 7, and 
most locations East of the Divide would likely remain dry 
through at least Saturday evening. As for the trick or treating 
weather, most guidance shows mainly dry conditions for most of 
the area Saturday evening with at most a 1 in 4 chance and that 
would be in the far west. It will be another fairly mild day as 
well. So, things look good for all the kiddos to get their 
annual sugar rush from the various forms of candy (save a 
Snickers bar for me).

All eyes are still looking at what will happen Sunday into Monday. 
We continue to have a complex set up, and details still remain 
somewhat uncertain at this time. There is a bit more agreement at 
this time though with the general pattern. The two main players are 
an upper level low that will drop southward along the Pacific 
Northwest Coast and move onshore in northern California Saturday 
night and another, much wetter low that will move onshore in 
southern California on Sunday. It looks like these two systems will 
phase to the south of Wyoming and continue East, with lee 
cyclogenesis occurring over Colorado Sunday night. The deepest 
moisture will remain to the south of Wyoming, over the desert 
southwest and over portions of Utah and Colorado. This should keep 
amounts down somewhat. And continuing the trend, the system is 
slower. All areas will have a chance of showers on Sunday, but most 
will be across western Wyoming. The wettest period looks to be 
Sunday night into Monday morning as the low moves eastward. There is 
a new wrinkle in a few of the models for Monday. It is that some 
ensemble runs, as well as the operational European model, show a 
good area of wrap around moisture that could impact areas East of 
the Divide Monday into Monday night. This is the first run showing 
it though, so I'm not completely buying into it yet. We will 
continue to watch it though to see if it persists though.

Now we move on the precipitation amounts, in the 48 hour period 
ending Tuesday at 6 am, the NBM ensemble guidance shows most areas 
having at least a 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch of 
precipitation, with the highest chance in the mountains. Areas with 
a greater than 1 out of 2 chance of 0.75 inches or more are 
generally confined to the mountains. The greatest chance will be in 
the western mountains, where a period of orographic enhancing 
westerly flow will bring heavier amounts, as well as in the  
Bighorn Range, more from the possible wrap around moisture. 

And the question more people are wondering about, will there be snow 
and how much and where? One change today is the most guidance has 
trended warmer, so the chance of accumulating snow in the lower 
elevations is looking less likely (less than a 1 out of 3 chance at 
this time). Snow levels look to remain fairly high through Saturday 
night. The 700 millibar temperatures are expected to remain 
near to above 0 degrees celsius, putting snow levels at 8500 
feet or higher. This could still impact some mountain passes 
though, especially Togwotee Pass. Colder air then moves into the
area as the low passes and flow turns to the north. There is
